title: Birth in Portland, Maine; parents and mother's piano career
summary: Leeman gives his birth date, his father Merle (a teamster) and mother Margaret Webb; the parents divorce around 1918-19 and his talented pianist mother pursues a career.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: My name is Clifford Leeman, and I was born in Portland, Maine, 1913, September 10th. And my Social Security number is 120-07-0590. My residence for the last 27, 28 years has been 21-04 154th Street, Whitestone, New York 11357, and I've lived in the same house for 27 years.
Beautiful. And your parent's name was Cliff?

Well, my father's name was Merle, Merle Leeman. And my mother's maiden name was Margaret Webb -- W-e-b-b. They were both from Maine, my father was born in Portland, Maine, as was I. My mother, I believe, was born in Portland, Maine. I have that all in the family Bible. I have a real old Bible that goes back to the early 1800's, by the way.
What kind of work did your father do?
My father was a Teamster, as they

were called in the days before trucking. He owned his own trucking business, and my grandfather was a Temaster who had his own trucking business, but that was before mobile automobiles, or trucks -- and I was born -- I was in the middle of the city of Portland, Maine, with my grandfolks, after my father and mother divorced, and I was brought up by my grandfolks.
My mother was a very talented pianist, and she -- why they broke up, I was only 5 or 6 years old, it was 1919, and I don't exactly know, except they were, as they say today, incompatible.

My mother then went on to have a career -- she went on to study the organ, and she was a very fine pianist as far as concert work, and especially she played in theatres, and what I heard of my mother, she played some ragtime, which I didn't know what it was at the time. Her approach to the piano, she made some rolls, piano rolls at one time -- and her approach to the piano, when she played personally, it sounded a great deal like a piano player, like a Ralph Sutton approach, or who was that fellow who used to be with the Bob Crosby band?
It was a 'Little Rock Getaway' approach, it was a heavy approach, I don't want to say she played like Bob Zurke
a man, but that was way, way back in the old days -- that's what people used to say, it was some old fashioned phrase, it was a very definite heavy approach.
When did you say your mother and father separated?
That was in 1918, during the war.
